A.explanation: This describes Hooke's law behaviour with $F = kx$, which is only a special case of elastic deformation up to the limit of proportionality.

B.explanation: Non-proportional extension can still be elastic if the wire returns to its original length after the elastic limit of proportionality but before the elastic limit.

C.explanation: Failure to return to the original length after the tensile force is removed describes plastic deformation with permanent set.

D.explanation: Elastic deformation is reversible deformation, so removal of the tensile force allows the wire to return to its original length.

hints: Focus on the words elastic deformation and when the tensile force is removed in the stem and in options C and D.
Recall that elastic means the deformation is reversible, while proportional means the $force$-$extension$ graph is a straight line through the origin.
Ask whether a wire loaded beyond the limit of proportionality but still below the elastic limit would still spring back to its original length.
walkthrough: Identify the key test in the question: a wire is pulled by a tensile force and then the force is removed, so check what happens to the extension.
State the governing definition: elastic deformation is reversible deformation where the material returns to its original shape and length when the load is removed.
Distinguish this from Hooke's law: extension proportional to force is a stricter condition that holds only up to the limit of proportionality.
Note that a wire can be non-proportional yet still elastic between the limit of proportionality and the elastic limit, so proportionality is not required.
Therefore only returning to the original length when the tensile force is removed matches elastic deformation. This is option D
